title: The Pipe Organ
objective: After this level you can explain how a pipe organ makes sound from air.
summary: Organs blow air into pipes, one per key in each rank; flue pipes use an air jet, reed pipes a reed; stops add ranks. Double a pipe's length, an octave down; lowest about 16 Hz.

cards.headline: The deepest organ pipes go below the floor of human hearing.
cards.body: Large pipe organs can sound notes as low as about 16 Hz. Remember Level 3: human hearing bottoms out at about 20 Hz. So how does one instrument, built from nothing but pipes and air, reach that low?

cards.headline: A keyboard that plays pipes
cards.body: An organ is a wind instrument with a keyboard. Bellows or a blower push pressurized air toward the pipes. A basic organ has one rank, a row with one pipe for each key. Press a key and air flows into that key's pipe. Each pipe sounds only its own note, which is why an organ needs so many of them.

cards.headline: Two kinds of pipe, many stops
cards.body: Remember Level 13's woodwinds? The organ uses their tricks. In a flue pipe, a jet of air vibrates against an edge, as in a flute. In a reed pipe, a metal reed vibrates, much as a reed does in a clarinet. Most organs have several ranks, called stops. Draw a stop and its whole rank joins in, adding a new voice to every key.

cards.fact: Double a pipe's length and its note drops an octave.
cards.context: An 8-foot pipe sounds at normal keyboard pitch; a 16-foot pipe sounds an octave lower, and a 4-foot pipe an octave higher. Pipes run from 32 feet down to less than an inch, giving an organ a possible range of nine octaves. That's Level 8's doubling, built into the pipes.

cards.headline: Organ: blown by machine
learned: Pressurized air, one pipe per key in each rank
Flue pipes: an air jet; reed pipes: a reed
Draw a stop to add a rank
Double the length, an octave down; lowest about 16 Hz

questions.prompt: On a pipe organ, what happens when the player draws a stop?

options.label: The organ plays a note an octave higher
options.rationale: Pipe length sets the octave, not the stop itself.

options.label: All the notes stop sounding
options.rationale: A stop adds pipes; it doesn't silence them.

options.label: Air stops flowing to the bellows
A whole rank of pipes joins in

questions.explanation: Each stop controls a rank of pipes; drawing it brings that rank into play.

questions.prompt: An 8-foot organ pipe sounds at normal keyboard pitch. How does a 16-foot pipe sound?

options.label: The same note, louder
options.rationale: Doubling the length changes the pitch.

questions.explanation: Doubling a pipe's length drops its note an octave: 16 feet sounds an octave below 8 feet.

questions.prompt: Level 3 said human hearing spans about 20 Hz to 20 kHz. How do the lowest notes of a large organ compare?

options.label: They reach about 16 Hz, below that floor
They stop at about 440 Hz
options.rationale: That's the tuning A, far above an organ's lowest notes.

options.label: They are above 20 kHz
options.rationale: Those would be too high, not too low.

options.label: They are exactly 20 Hz, the limit

questions.explanation: Large pipe organs reach notes as low as about 16 Hz, below the roughly 20 Hz bottom of human hearing.
